write.desc: This topic covers the tools for studying a sequence through its parts and its tails, without knowing its limit in advance: subsequences, the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, Cauchy sequences and the Cauchy criterion, and limit superior and limit inferior. They belong together because each one builds on the one before: Bolzano-Weierstrass extracts convergent subsequences, the Cauchy criterion is proved from it, and limsup and liminf describe the largest and smallest subsequential limits.

points.name: Subsequences
points.what: Define a subsequence (a_{n_k}) using a strictly increasing sequence of indices n_1 < n_2 < ..., tell subsequences apart from sequences that are not subsequences (repeated or reordered terms), and prove by induction that n_k >= k.
outside: a sequence as a function from the natural numbers to the reals

points.name: Subsequences of a convergent sequence
points.what: Prove from the epsilon-N definition that every subsequence of a sequence converging to L also converges to L, using n_k >= k to carry the N over from the sequence to the subsequence.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Proving divergence with subsequences
points.what: Prove that a sequence diverges by finding two subsequences with different limits, or one subsequence that does not converge, for example (-1)^n or sin(n pi / 3), and explain why this works.

points.name: Every sequence has a monotone subsequence
points.what: Prove the peak-point lemma: using peak terms (terms larger than every later term), every real sequence has a monotone subsequence, splitting into the cases of infinitely many and finitely many peaks.

points.name: The Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem
points.what: State and prove that every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence, by combining the monotone subsequence lemma with the monotone convergence theorem, and see that the limit is not named in advance.

points.name: Bolzano-Weierstrass by bisection
points.what: Prove Bolzano-Weierstrass a second way: repeatedly halve an interval containing the sequence, keep a half holding infinitely many terms, pick one term from each interval with increasing indices, and use the nested interval property to find the limit of the chosen subsequence.

points.name: Subsequential limits
points.what: Define a subsequential limit (limit point of a sequence), find all of them for examples such as (-1)^n + 1/n, and prove that a bounded sequence converges exactly when all its convergent subsequences have the same limit.

points.name: Cauchy sequences
points.what: State the definition of a Cauchy sequence (for every epsilon > 0 there is N with |a_m - a_n| < epsilon for all m, n >= N), compare it with the definition of convergence, which needs a limit L, and prove that every Cauchy sequence is bounded.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Convergent sequences are Cauchy
points.what: Prove with the epsilon/2 technique that every convergent sequence is Cauchy, by passing through the limit: |a_m - a_n| <= |a_m - L| + |L - a_n|.
outside: epsilon/2 technique for splitting a bound

points.name: The Cauchy criterion
points.what: Prove that every Cauchy sequence of reals converges: Bolzano-Weierstrass gives a convergent subsequence, and the Cauchy property pulls the whole sequence to its limit. Understand that this lets one prove convergence without knowing or guessing the limit.

points.name: Cauchy criterion and completeness
points.what: Give a Cauchy sequence of rationals with no rational limit, such as the decimal truncations of sqrt 2. Explain that the Cauchy criterion is a form of completeness that holds in the reals but not in the rationals, alongside the supremum axiom, the nested interval property and monotone convergence.

points.name: Contractive sequences
points.what: Prove that a contractive sequence, with |a_{n+1} - a_n| <= c|a_n - a_{n-1}| for a fixed c < 1, is Cauchy and so converges, by bounding |a_m - a_n| with a geometric sum. Apply this to a recursion such as a_{n+1} = 1/(2 + a_n), including an error bound for the limit.

points.name: Limit superior and limit inferior
points.what: For a bounded sequence, define limsup a_n and liminf a_n as the limits of the decreasing sequence sup_{k>=n} a_k and the increasing sequence inf_{k>=n} a_k, prove that both limits exist and that liminf <= limsup, and compute them for examples.
outside: supremum and infimum of a set

points.name: Epsilon characterisation of limsup and liminf
points.what: Prove and use the characterisation: for every epsilon > 0, a_n < limsup + epsilon for all large n, and a_n > limsup - epsilon for infinitely many n, with the matching statement for liminf.
outside: approximation property of the supremum (sup - epsilon is not an upper bound)

points.name: limsup and liminf as extreme subsequential limits
points.what: Prove that limsup a_n is the largest subsequential limit and liminf a_n the smallest, by building a subsequence that converges to limsup and showing that no subsequence can have a larger limit.

points.name: Convergence exactly when limsup equals liminf
points.what: Prove that a bounded sequence converges if and only if limsup a_n = liminf a_n, and that the common value is then the limit, by squeezing a_n between the tail infimum and the tail supremum.

points.name: limsup and liminf of unbounded sequences
points.what: Extend limsup and liminf to every sequence using plus and minus infinity (limsup = +infinity exactly when the sequence is unbounded above), and check that the earlier results still hold, including that a_n tends to +infinity exactly when liminf a_n = +infinity.
outside: divergence of a sequence to plus or minus infinity
